--- title: 7 Linear regression --- In this lesson we will learn how to perform a simple linear regression by examining the counts, weight, and size measurements of juvenile snowshoe hares (*Lepus americanus*) observed at the Bonanza Creek Experimental Forest from 1998 to 2012 @kielland_snowshoe_2017. ## Learning objectives By the end of this lesson, students will be able to: - Explore a dataset's values against its metadata and document data cleaning decisions. - Create plots with multiple layers using `matplotlib`'s `fig` and `ax`. - Fit a simple linear regression with `statsmodels` using a formula. - Interpret the intercept, slope and $R^2$ of a linear regression model. - Use residuals to assess whether a linear model is a good description of the data. ## About the data Size measurements, sex, and age of snowshoe hares were collected and made available by Dr. Knut Kielland and colleagues at the [Bonanza Creek Experimental Forest Long Term Ecological Research (LTER) site](https://www.lter.uaf.edu) located approximately 20 km southwest of Fairbanks, Alaska, USA. The data contains 3380 observations (captures) of snowshoe hares obtained by capture-recapture studies conducted yearly from 1998 to 2012 in three sampling sites: Bonanza Riparian, Bonanza Mature and Bonanza Black Spruce. ![Photo credit: Jim Dau, [Alaska Department of Fish and Game.](https://www.adfg.alaska.gov/index.cfm?adfg=snowshoehare.main)](/book/images/lesson-18/snowshoehare_boards.jpg) ## Data exploration Download the `55_Hare_Data_2012.txt` file [available here]({{< var hares-data-folder >}}) and save it in a `data/` folder next to your notebook. This is the same file used in discussion section 3: a copy of `55_Hare_Data_2012.txt` from version 22 of the EDI data package. Let's start by loading the data and taking a very high-level look at it: ::: {#8e2e8e50 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import os import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import statsmodels.formula.api as smf ``` ::: ::: {#ed1cf465 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} obs = pd.read_csv(os.path.join('data','55_Hare_Data_2012.txt')) obs.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=42} ```{=html}

Other columns as `weight` and `hindft` contain continuous numerical variables. To facilitate our data wrangling we convert the `date` column to a `datetime` type: ::: {#0b82bac6 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} obs['date'] = pd.to_datetime(obs['date']) print(obs['date'].dtype) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` datetime64[ns] ``` ::: ::: ## Examining hares' age data From the data's `info()` display we can see that the `age` column has 1269 non-NA rows. In this example we are interested in working with data from juvenile hares exclusively. So we will: 1. Examine the values in the `age` column 2. Filter for observations in which age is 'adult' or 'juvenile' 3. Investigate the age distributions across time From the [dataset's metadata](https://portal.edirepository.org/nis/metadataviewer?packageid=knb-lter-bnz.55.22) we know there are three allowed values in the `age` column: - 'a' for 'adult', - 'j' for 'juvenile', and - 'm' for 'mortality'. Let's see the data in this column: ::: {#6af0fbc7 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Examine unique values and counts in age column pd.DataFrame(obs['age'].value_counts(dropna=False)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=45} ```{=html}

Since the actual data has values that are not included in the metadata, this is the time to make a decision and document it. Since the metadata states that 'a' indicates adult and 'j' indicates juvenile, we will only keep observations that have 'a' or 'j' (either capitalized or not) as part of the age value. ::: {#616daca4 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Update age values to juvenile and adult for observations where 'a' and 'j' are included obs.loc[obs['age'].str.contains('j', case=False, na=False), 'age'] = 'juvenile' obs.loc[obs['age'].str.contains('a', case=False, na=False), 'age'] = 'adult' # Filter for confirmed observations of juvenile and adult hares obs_juv_adult = obs[obs['age'].isin(['juvenile', 'adult'])].copy() print("Number of juvenile and adult hare observations (captures):", len(obs_juv_adult)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Number of juvenile and adult hare observations (captures): 1155 ``` ::: ::: None of the observations from 1998 have a valid age, so from here on our data starts in 1999. To better understand our data we examine the distribution of hare age across years. Let's wrangle our data a bit to get there: ::: {#532a647d .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Extract year in which each observation happened obs_juv_adult['year'] = obs_juv_adult['date'].dt.year # Count observations per year and age, then move age values into columns obs_per_year = obs_juv_adult.groupby(['year', 'age']).size().unstack() obs_per_year ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=47} ```{=html}

In this format it is easy to create a stacked bar plot to examine the occurrence of juvenile and adult hares: ::: {#347ca5fb .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} obs_per_year[['juvenile', 'adult']].plot(kind='bar', # Columns in stacking order stacked=True, # Stack the bars color=['#8FBC8F', '#4682B4'], title='Juvenile and adult snowshoe hare captures per year', xlabel='Year', ylabel='Number of captures'); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-18-linear-regression_files/figure-html/cell-9-output-1.png){width=593 height=470} ::: ::: No observations of juvenile snowshoe hares were made during 2002, while the highest count was registered in 1999 (the first year of the study) with 126 observations. In the previous plot we can see that the number of juvenile hare trappings dropped sharply from 1999 to 2002 and stayed lower for the rest of the study, with peaks in 2005, 2008, and 2011. :::{.callout-tip} # Check-in Consider the following questions: - In what ways could the data collection methods affect the results we see here? - Is there additional metadata you would need to better understand the data? ::: ## Plotting with `matplotlib` ### `matplotlib`'s `fig` and `ax` Later in this lesson we will want to plot our linear model together with our data. To make visualizations where we add different layers to a graph and customize it, we will use the `matplotlib` Python library for creating visualizations. We can interact with `matplotlib` via its `pyplot` interface, which we imported at the top of the notebook. Matplotlib graphs the data in a **figure** which can have one or more **axes**. The axes is *only* the area specified by the $x$ axis and $y$ axis and what is plotted in it, while the figure can include multiple axes in it. ![Image source: [Getting Started with Matplotlib.](https://www.skytowner.com/explore/getting_started_with_matplotlib)](/book/images/lesson-10/matplotlib_figure_axes_axis.png) To create a new blank figure: 1. Initialize a new figure and axes by calling `pyplot`'s `subplots()` function 2. Display the figure using `plt.show()`: ::: {#8975546a .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Initialize empty figure (fig) and axis (ax) fig, ax = plt.subplots() # Display figure plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-18-linear-regression_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-1.png){width=581 height=416} ::: ::: Notice that `plt.subplots()` is a function that returns two objects, when we call it, we get a figure `fig` with a single empty axis `ax`. We can think of this step as setting a new blank canvas on which we will paint upon. ### Adding a layer When using `matplotlib`, it can be useful to think of creating a plot as adding layers to an axis. The general syntax to plot data from a data frame `df` onto an axis is: ```python # Initialize empty figure and axis fig, ax = plt.subplots() # Plot df on the ax axis df.plot(ax=ax, # Add plot to axis ...) # Other arguments for plot function # Display figure plt.show() ``` For example, let's add a scatter plot of the hind foot length and weight of all the juvenile and adult captures to our axis: ::: {#a7264e17 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Initialize empty figure and axis fig, ax = plt.subplots() # Add scatter plot of hares' data to our figure's axis obs_juv_adult.plot(kind='scatter', x='hindft', y='weight', ax=ax) # Display figure plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-18-linear-regression_files/figure-html/cell-11-output-1.png){width=602 height=429} ::: ::: ### Customization Matplotlib allows for a lot of customization. Some of it can be done directly in the `plot()` method for the data frame (like we've done when plotting data using `pandas`), while other is done by updating attributes of the `ax` axis. The following diagram shows some examples of elements in the axis that can be updated. ![Image source: Matplotlib documentation.](/book/images/lesson-10/anatomy.png){width="70%"} For example, we can update the title and axis labels of our previous plot like this: ::: {#c970f742 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Initialize empty figure and axis fig, ax = plt.subplots() # Add data to axis obs_juv_adult.plot(kind='scatter', x='hindft', y='weight', alpha=0.5, # Adjust transparency ax=ax) # Add plot to axis # Update axis ax.set_title('Hind foot length and weight of snowshoe hares') ax.set_xlabel('Hind foot length (mm)') ax.set_ylabel('Weight (g)') # Display figure plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-18-linear-regression_files/figure-html/cell-12-output-1.png){width=602 height=449} ::: ::: ## Linear regression For our analysis we want to investigate possible relations between hind foot length and weight for juvenile hares. Let's take a look at our target data: ::: {#34a1f7c4 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Subset juvenile hares and drop rows missing hind foot or weight measurements juveniles_weight_hindft = obs_juv_adult[obs_juv_adult['age'] == 'juvenile'].dropna(subset=['hindft', 'weight']) print("Number of juvenile hare captures with hind foot and weight measurements:", len(juveniles_weight_hindft)) juveniles_weight_hindft.plot.scatter(x='hindft', y='weight', alpha=0.5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Number of juvenile hare captures with hind foot and weight measurements: 265 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-18-linear-regression_files/figure-html/cell-13-output-2.png){width=602 height=429} ::: ::: Remember from our bar plot that the number of captures changed a lot from year to year: our regression combines juveniles from all years, and almost a third of them (79 of 265) were captured in 1999. We can see there seems to be a linear trend between the weight and hind foot length variables, though as the hind foot length increases the variability does too. Let's investigate whether a linear model is an adequate way to describe this data. To do this we will use the [`statsmodels`](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/index.html) library, which has tools for fitting statistical models. At the top of the notebook we imported it as `smf`. Remember that in statistical notation the linear regression model is $$y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \epsilon,$$ where $x$ = the **predictor** variable, $y$ is the **response** variable, and $\epsilon \sim Normal(0, \sigma)$. Once we estimate the coefficients from the data, the equation of the fitted line is $$\hat{y} = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 x, $$ where - $\hat{y}$ = the **estimated value of the response** $y$ at $x$ from the linear model - $\hat\beta_0$ = the **$y$-intercept** of the linear model, this is interpreted as the estimated average value of the response when the predictor is $x=0$ - $\hat\beta_1$ = the **slope** of the linear model, this is the estimated difference in the response $\hat{y}$ per unit of the predictor $x$. If you need a refresher about how a linear regression works, [click here](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/model-slr.html) for a great resource. To fit the model we use the [`ols()`](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/generated/statsmodels.formula.api.ols.html) function, short for **ordinary least squares**, the method that finds the line that minimizes the sum of the squared vertical distances between the data points and the line. It takes two arguments: - a **formula** of the form `'response ~ predictor'`, a string that we can read as "response explained by predictor". The names in the formula are the names of the columns in our data frame. - `data`: the data frame with those columns. `ols()` sets up the model, and calling `fit()` on it estimates the coefficients: ::: {#508ae687 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Fit model: weight explained by hind foot length model = smf.ols('weight ~ hindft', data=juveniles_weight_hindft).fit() ``` ::: The estimated coefficients are stored in the model's `params` attribute, a `pandas.Series` whose index has the names of the coefficients: ::: {#650ef926 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} model.params ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=54} ``` Intercept -352.771986 hindft 10.092240 dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: The `Intercept` value is $\hat\beta_0$ and the `hindft` value is $\hat\beta_1$, the slope for the hind foot length. Let's save them in variables to use them later: ::: {#3ee90b05 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Retrieve intercept and slope intercept = model.params['Intercept'] print("y-intercept:", intercept) slope = model.params['hindft'] print("Slope:", slope) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` y-intercept: -352.77198564640645 Slope: 10.092239638623006 ``` ::: ::: :::{.callout-tip} # Exercise Answer the following questions: a. What would be the biological meaning of the $y$-intercept? Does it make sense to use it as such? b. What is the estimated change in weight for each millimeter increase in hind foot length? Write your answer in a full sentence. c. Estimate the weight of a juvenile hare with hind foot length of 90 mm. Is this a reasonable use of the model? ::: We can also look at the **coefficient of determination**, $R^2$. This is between 0 and 1, with $R^2=1$ describing a perfect fit of the model to the data. The $R^2$ value is interpreted as the proportion of variance in the response $y$ that is explained by the least squares line with the predictor $x$. This value is stored in the model's `rsquared` attribute: ::: {#02236ed6 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} print("R^2:", model.rsquared) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` R^2: 0.3871164783665738 ``` ::: ::: :::{.callout-tip} # Check-in Answer the following questions: - Does a linear model of weight with respect to hind foot length account completely for the change in the response? - How would you further explore whether this model is a good fit for the data? ::: A reasonable next step would be to plot our linear model together with our data. To do this, we need to add two layers to the same graph: the data points and the regression line. To draw the line we use the axis's `plot()` method, `ax.plot(x_values, y_values)`, which connects the points given by the lists of $x$ and $y$ values. A straight line only needs two points, so we use the smallest and largest hind foot lengths and calculate their estimated weights with the equation of the linear model, $\hat{y} = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 x$: ::: {#a33e15f9 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Smallest and largest hind foot lengths x_start = juveniles_weight_hindft['hindft'].min() x_end = juveniles_weight_hindft['hindft'].max() # Initialize empty figure and axis fig, ax = plt.subplots() # Add data to axis juveniles_weight_hindft.plot(kind='scatter', x='hindft', y='weight', alpha=0.5, # Adjust transparency ax=ax) # Add plot to axis # Add regression line to axis ax.plot([x_start, x_end], [intercept + slope*x_start, intercept + slope*x_end], color='darkred') # Update axis ax.set_title('Hind foot length and weight of juvenile snowshoe hares') ax.set_xlabel('Hind foot length (mm)') ax.set_ylabel('Weight (g)') # Display figure plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-18-linear-regression_files/figure-html/cell-18-output-1.png){width=602 height=449} ::: ::: ## Checking the residuals $R^2$ tells us how much of the variation the model explains, but not whether a straight line is the right shape for the data. One check for this is looking at the **residuals**. A residual is the difference between an observed value and the value predicted by the model: $$e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i.$$ The residuals are the $\epsilon$ in our model equation, so the model assumes they are normally distributed around 0, with the same standard deviation $\sigma$ for every value of the predictor. `statsmodels` calculates the residuals for us and stores them in the model's `resid` attribute. ::: {#f69d90a3 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} model.resid ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=58} ``` 108 -523.850209 109 -609.864845 110 -655.510522 111 -397.835573 112 -549.403647 ... 3355 -46.820937 3359 117.625625 3360 117.625625 3367 -276.175259 3369 -37.189895 Length: 265, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: Let's start with a histogram to see their distribution: ::: {#790db53a .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} model.resid.plot(kind='hist', bins=30, title='Distribution of residuals', xlabel='Residual (g)') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-18-linear-regression_files/figure-html/cell-20-output-1.png){width=593 height=449} ::: ::: The residuals are centered near 0 and roughly bell-shaped, but with a long tail of negative residuals: some hares weigh much less than the line predicts. Let's see where these residuals come from. If a linear model describes the data well, the residuals should be scattered randomly around 0, with about the same spread for every value of $x$. Let's plot them against the hind foot length. Since the residuals are not a column of our data frame, we plot them with the axis's `scatter()` method, `ax.scatter(x_values, y_values)`. We also add a horizontal reference line at 0 with `ax.axhline()`: ::: {#639760b5 .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Initialize empty figure and axis fig, ax = plt.subplots() # Add residuals to axis ax.scatter(juveniles_weight_hindft['hindft'], model.resid, alpha=0.5) # Add reference line at 0 ax.axhline(0, color='darkred', linestyle='--') # Update axis ax.set_title('Residuals of the linear model') ax.set_xlabel('Hind foot length (mm)') ax.set_ylabel('Residual (g)') # Display figure plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-18-linear-regression_files/figure-html/cell-21-output-1.png){width=604 height=449} ::: ::: The residuals show three patterns: - **The spread grows with hind foot length.** For short hind feet most residuals are within about 100 g of 0, while for the longest hind feet many are more than 300 g away. This is the increasing variability we noticed in the first scatter plot. It means the model's predictions are less precise for larger juveniles. - **The residuals are not centered on 0 everywhere.** For hind feet shorter than about 100 mm most residuals are negative (the line overestimates weight), while for medium hind feet they are mostly positive (the line underestimates weight). This suggests that the relationship between hind foot length and weight is not exactly linear. - **For longer hind feet the residuals split into two groups**, one above and one below the line. This could mean that another variable also affects weight. None of these patterns means the model is useless: the line still captures the overall trend. But they are a reminder that a single $R^2$ value doesn't tell the whole story, and that we should be careful when using the model to make predictions, especially for larger juveniles. :::{.callout-tip} # Check-in - For longer hind feet, the residuals split into two groups. Looking at the columns in our data, which variables could explain these groups? - Each row in our data is a capture, and some hares were captured more than once. Are two captures of the same hare independent observations? How could this affect our model? ::: ## Wrap-up In this lesson we fit a simple linear regression of juvenile snowshoe hare weight on hind foot length. Before modeling, we explored the data and documented how we handled the `age` values that didn't match the metadata. We then used `statsmodels` to estimate the intercept and slope, measured the fit with $R^2$, and plotted the fitted line with `matplotlib`. Finally, the residuals showed that while the line captures the overall trend, the spread grows with hind foot length and other variables may also affect weight. Fitting a model is only the first step: checking it against the data tells us how far we can trust it!
